The attributes selected for separate attention are structural serviceability, structural safety, health and safety, fire safety, acoustical environment, illuminated environment, durability/time reliability, and spatial characteristics and arrangement.
The "built elements" which must perform satisfactorily with respect to these attributes and the defined requirements are the structure, interior walls and doors (both inter- and intra-dwelling unit), floor-ceiling envelope, exterior walls and openings, experior ceiling-roof envelope, fixtures and hardware, plumbing, mechanical equipment, electrical system, lighting elements, and enclosed spaces.
In establishing the Guide Criteria, care was taken to first quantify that level of performance expected from acceptable existing construction; where appropriate, particularly in the area of fire protection and acoustical environment, performance standards were developed to fill a gap in most existing specifications and codes.
The Guide Criteria are still considered an evolving document, with comments of professional and industry groups now being considered for inclusion in any revision of the document. Also, experience in the use and application of performance—oriented requirements is being applied to revisions of other Departmental standards for design and construction.
g) Quality Control and Testing: To insure that the housing produced under this program is in fact safe, sound, durable and livable, HUD has required each of the systems producers to establish and use formal quality assurance programs, and monitored this effort through the agency of a "third party inspector", selected in one of the competitive procurements noted earlier. Parallel to this activity, HUD also obtained the services of NBS to review the detailed designs against the Guide Criteria, and then to conduct or monitor testing programs where experience or prior evidence was insufficient to judge performance of a material or an assembly.
ii. Prototype Sites
a) Relationship to Communities: The prototype sites are intended to be examples of effective design of a community in which a mix of housing types, including both single- and multi-family units with various price levels, can be arranged without sacrificing a good living environment. The first task of the site planners was to investigate the existing site condition and the surrounding community environment, and from this data develop a conceptual plan for the site. Consideration was given to the neighborhood characteristics, and in every site, the site planners made presentations of the program and the conceptual site plan to interested community groups.
